facts.claim: [Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues 03-source-pack, same source and date.] The Municipality of Rhodes (rhodes.gr) publishes a page, in Greek, listing the supporting documents for performing a civil marriage of foreign nationals (under article 5(1) of Presidential Decree 391/1982): a joint application by the couple; a marriage licence or a certificate of no impediment to marriage from the person's consular or other public authority, naming the person they will marry, valid for six months; a copy of each passport; a municipal fee (a fee applies); and a form with the newlyweds' details. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_01, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues 03-source-pack, same source and date.] The Municipality of Rhodes page states that documents issued by foreign authorities must be originals of recent issue and officially translated into Greek, by a Greek lawyer, by the Greek Embassy abroad or by the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and that for countries outside the European Union they require certification with the Apostille stamp. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_02, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues 03-source-pack, same source and date.] The Municipality of Rhodes page states that details not shown on the documents provided can be recorded after the couple files a solemn declaration under Law 1599/1986, using the municipality's template. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_03, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Municipal conditions stated (Registry Office, Municipality of Rhodes): required documents include a full birth certificate translated into Greek, valid marriage licences or certificates of no impediment naming both partners and the wedding place, divorce or death certificates where relevant, a residence permit for non-EU countries, and passport copies; documents need an Apostille where applicable, also translated into Greek. Originals must be presented to the registrar two days before the wedding. A fee applies, payable at the registry office. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_04, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues 03-source-pack, same source and date.] The municipal page says the Town Hall of Rhodes ceremony takes place every Wednesday and Friday, with the couple returning to the registry office the next working day to sign and have the marriage certificate drawn up, and that two adult witnesses over 18 must be present. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_05, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, the Australian Embassy in Athens lists among its notarial services: witnessing application forms for, and issuing of, Certificates of No Impediment (CNI); witnessing notices of intended marriage; and legalisation of signatures and/or seals by authentication or apostille (original Australian public documents only). [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_07, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Australian Embassy Athens: an appointment is required for all notarial services (Monday to Friday, 9:00 am to 12:30 pm), though Apostille and CNI documents may be submitted by post; legalised documents and CNIs are available for collection within two working days unless otherwise arranged. A fee applies. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_08, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Australian Embassy Athens: it does not provide legal advice, the onus is on the client to present documents in the correct form, it does not witness signatures on overseas documents, and Honorary Consuls cannot provide notarial services. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_09, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Australian Embassy, Athens: 5 Hatziyianni Mexi Street, Athens 115 28; phone +30 210 870 4000; greece.embassy.gov.au. [Copied from greek-wedding-traditions part-1 fact_102.] [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-1 fact_105.] [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_10, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller (read live 11 November 2026) says DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia, but some local authorities only accept CNIs issued in their country, so ask the destination's embassy or consulate whether you need a CNI, whether you can get it in Australia, and whether it also needs an authentication or apostille. [Copied from mykonos-wedding part-1 fact_101.] [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-1 fact_106.] [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_11, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (last updated 18/08/2026, read live 12 November 2026): some countries ask you to prove you aren't already married; the most common documents are a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) and certificates from a registry of births, deaths and marriages; the country may have more rules (for example a residence period); 'We can't tell you what you will need'; contact your destination's embassy or consulate. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_12, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (read live 12 November 2026): your registry of births, deaths and marriages can give a statement that there's no record you have been married before, a Single Status certificate or a No Record Result certificate; local authorities may also ask for divorce papers, the death certificate of a deceased spouse, and your original birth certificate and passport. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_13, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (read live 12 November 2026): Australia doesn't recognise overseas marriages where one or both people are already married to someone else, not old enough to get married, too closely related, or forced to get married. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_14, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, Smartraveller (read live 11 November 2026) says you cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if, when it took place, it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia. A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage but may not work as proof of a name change (check with your local registry of births, deaths and marriages), and Smartraveller suggests talking to a lawyer to confirm the certificate is valid in Australia. [Copied from mykonos-wedding part-1 fact_102.] [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-1 fact_108.] [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_15, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from same-sex-marriage-greece 03-source-pack, same source and date.] As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department (read live 12 November 2026): if Australia recognises your overseas marriage, you can't get married again in Australia, but you may choose to hold another type of ceremony, such as a confirmation of vows or a recommitment ceremony. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_16, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from santorini-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Smartraveller (DFAT), 'How to get your documents legalised' (last updated 30/09/2026): ask the overseas authority which documents they need and which must be legalised; DFAT 'can't tell you what they may want'. Find out from the intended authority or legal representative whether you need an apostille or an authentication certificate. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_17, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from santorini-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Smartraveller: documents that are not original Australian public documents must first be notarised by an Australian Notary Public; the apostille or authentication certificate is applied directly to the document, so if you don't want originals marked, get a notarised copy legalised (and check the overseas authority accepts it). [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_18, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from santorini-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Smartraveller: requests use the Document Legalisation Request Form, signed in front of an authorised witness, and can be lodged by appointment at an Australian Passport Office, in person at many Australian embassies, high commissions and consulates overseas (not Honorary Consul consulates), or by registered mail to the Authentications Section in Melbourne or Sydney. A fee applies (amount not recorded). [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_19, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from santorini-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Smartraveller: processing times vary, with delays at the end of the school year and in peak holiday periods, for incomplete requests or unpaid fees, or when the issuing authority must be contacted. An Australian-issued apostille can be verified online via DFAT. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_20, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: weddings are performed by a Priest recognised as canonical by the Archdiocese; the laws and regulations for weddings are set by the Holy Canons of the Orthodox Church and implemented by the Archdiocese, and apply to every Greek Orthodox Priest across Australia. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_21, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: every Greek Orthodox Priest in Australia is also a registered civil celebrant, authorised to conduct the marriage under both State and Ecclesiastical law, but may perform the civil marriage only together with the religious service on the same day. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_22, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the ceremony has two parts, the Betrothal Service with the blessing of the rings, and the Marriage Service with the crowning of the bride and groom. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_23, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: a marriage cannot take place in the Orthodox Church between an Orthodox Christian and a non-Christian; the non-Orthodox partner must belong to a Christian denomination acceptable to the Orthodox Church (the page lists them, including Roman Catholic, Anglican, Uniting, Lutheran and Presbyterian, and lists denominations whose members may not marry in the Church). A baptism performed by a female pastor or member of clergy is not accepted. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_24, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: people who are not Christian or were never baptised can only marry in the Orthodox Church after being baptised in a denomination acceptable to the Orthodox Church. A non-Orthodox spouse does not become a member of the Church and may not receive Holy Communion; non-Orthodox clergy may not co-celebrate. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_25, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: having been baptised in the name of the Holy Trinity, both parties are asked to declare that any children will be baptised in the Eastern Orthodox Church and raised in the Orthodox Faith. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_26, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: both parties must present a birth certificate (if born in Australia) or passport (if born overseas) and a baptismal certificate; Orthodox parties never married before need a Certificate of Celibacy ('Agamias') from their local parish priest, signed by two witnesses. Widowed parties provide the spouse's death certificate. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_27, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: divorcing parties need a civil divorce certificate and then an ecclesiastical divorce; for a second or third marriage, both divorces must be issued at least one calendar month before the next marriage. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_28, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the Notice of Intended Marriage (for the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages) and the Application to the Archdiocese must be completed in the presence of the Priest at least one calendar month before the wedding, preferably three months. The Parish Priest gives directions on documents and on Archdiocese and local church fees, which vary by circumstances. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_29, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: marriages are not permitted from 13 December until Christmas Day; on 5 January (eve of Epiphany); from Great Lent until Easter Sunday (dates vary each year); from 1 to 15 August (Dormition of the Theotokos); on 29 August; and on 14 September. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_30, same source, wording and checked date.]

[Copied from rhodes-wedding-venues 03-source-pack, same source and date.] Smartraveller (as at November 2026): Australians can travel to the Schengen area, which includes Greece, for short trips without a visa for up to 90 days in any 180-day period; the EES registers fingerprints and a photo on arrival, at no cost, and may cause border delays. Entry conditions can change at short notice; contact the nearest Greek embassy or consulate. [Reused from content/posts/getting-married-in-greece/03-source-pack.json fact_31, same source, wording and checked date.]

As at November 2026, Smartraveller's Greece page says to get comprehensive travel insurance before you leave and closely read the Product Disclosure Statement (PDS); it must cover all medical costs overseas, including evacuation, which the Australian Government will not pay; if you can't afford travel insurance you shouldn't travel. There is no agreement between Australia and Greece for free healthcare, so tourists pay for all medical care, including hospital stays and evacuation, and payment is required before leaving the facility. Check the policy covers the whole trip including stopovers, and know the exclusions (some activities, such as going on a cruise, may cost extra to cover). insider_details.detail: Order the legal paperwork backwards from the Greek registrar: the Municipality of Rhodes wants recent originals, officially translated into Greek and carrying an Apostille for non-EU countries, shown to the registrar before the wedding. Australian public documents are legalised through DFAT, processing slows at the end of the school year and in peak holiday periods, and a fee applies at each step, so budget time as well as money for the paperwork.

Ask the chosen municipality early whether it accepts an Australian-issued CNI or wants one from the Australian Embassy in Athens. Smartraveller notes some authorities only accept CNIs issued in their own country, and the Embassy works by appointment on weekday mornings, so this choice shapes how many days the couple needs in Athens or on the island before the ceremony.

Build a working day after a civil ceremony into the stay: at Rhodes Town Hall the couple returns to the registry office the next working day to sign and have the marriage certificate drawn up. Extra nights for the couple are a real line item in the plan.

For a Greek Orthodox wedding, lock the church date before booking anything else: the Archdiocese of Australia rules out several fixed periods, including the first half of August and from Great Lent to Easter Sunday, which removes some peak-season dates from the calendar altogether.

Summer brings heatwaves, wildfire risk from June to September, crowded seaports and ferries that can be cancelled in strong winds. Plan shaded ceremony spaces, water for guests, pre-booked coaches or licensed taxis, and a buffer day for island guests, and remember each of these is part of what the wedding costs in high season.

Ask every supplier for the contract, deposit and cancellation terms in writing before paying. The ACCC says consumers are not entitled to a refund under the consumer guarantees for a change of mind, a refund after a major problem may not be in full, and getting a remedy from an overseas business can be difficult. Guests and the couple also need comprehensive travel insurance, because Australia and Greece have no agreement covering medical care.
